locator: 1.1.1 What does the Starter Kit do, p.9
paraphrase: Three step approach: identify relevant risks, run tests in a structured way from outputs to components, then assess results against baseline safety.
Developers and testers can use the guide to validate whether the app is safe and reliable; compliance staff can use it to judge sufficiency of testing.
Kit is aligned with AI Verify outcomes that recommend regular safety testing and testing for potential bias, and with NIST AI RMF MEASURE functions.
Test methodology must be rigorous and well designed for results to be credible; approach should combine output testing and component testing, via benchmarking and red teaming.
Benchmarks need to be complemented by red teaming for blind spots, rare failure modes and multi-turn scenarios; simulation based testing may also be considered.
Test dataset should represent the app's purpose, domain and anticipated usage, with realistic inputs, subject matter expert input, and about 30-50 prompts per narrow topic (100-200 wider).
Users can switch evaluators or define their own LLM-as-a-Judge criteria in the testing tool.
IMDA ran a multicultural, multilingual red teaming exercise across nine countries.
Automated red teaming uses an attacker LLM to iteratively probe and refine attacks; a case study tested an agency chatbot across priority behaviour categories.
Test depth should reflect reputational or legal exposure; even low risk apps should run simple tests on a small representative set; repeat tests and report average, minimum and maximum.
Each organisation must set its own thresholds before testing, with clear targets per risk scenario, refined and validated after testing.
Case study used ROUGE, FactScore and human evaluation as a final check.
Developers can use an open tool to build out of knowledge base robustness tests for their RAG pipeline.
Isolate the retriever and compare retrieved items to ground truth using precision and recall (recall first), or an LLM judge for relevance when no ground truth exists; keep references current.
Test whether output is grounded in retrieved information using a binary or percentage grounding score from a fine tuned model or LLM judge, reusing the output test dataset.
Case study tested an AML summariser with 400 multilingual samples including perturbed inputs, measuring precision of extracted facts.
Pick parity testing when groups and ground truth labels exist; perturbation testing when labels are unavailable or for specific updates.
Test and evaluate data and content flows.
Develop tests to identify synthetic content.
Evaluate training data quality and provenance using chaos engineering and stakeholder feedback.
Consider baseline benchmark performance when selecting a model for fine-tuning or RAG.
Verify training, TEVV and fine-tuning or RAG data provenance and grounding.
Regularly review safety and security guardrails.
Assess training data for bias, IP, privacy, obscenity, extremism and CBRN content.
Verify architecture monitors outputs and recovers from errors and anomalies.
Perform AI red teaming for resilience against attacks such as prompt injection, poisoning, extraction.
Assess ratio of synthetic to non-synthetic training data for homogeneity.
Assess safety to physical environments when deploying GAI systems.
Evaluate performance in real-world scenarios.
Decommission or retrain pre-trained models outside defined limits.

locator: Part 3 table, Data Governance: Non-personal data, p27
paraphrase: Recommends evaluating non-personal (e.g. copyrighted) data memorisation using a pre-processed HELM dataset and HELM.

Organisations should examine the tools used to decide which evaluations to re-conduct.
Additional evaluations are warranted for frontier model risks, on top of the baseline, using the latest tools and techniques.
Encourages organisations to minimally conduct the baseline evaluations before LLM release and deployment.
Defines testing in real-world conditions as temporary testing for intended purpose outside a laboratory, governed by a real-world testing plan.
Use of real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Art. 27 first.
A provider who concludes an Annex III system is not high-risk must document that assessment before placing it on the market.

locator: Part 2 C. Common Guiding Principles, 2) Safety (1), p.15-16
paraphrase: Ensure the AI system or service sufficiently meets requirements, including accuracy of outputs.

Decide whether unavoidable biases are acceptable from the viewpoint of respect for human rights.

locator: Part 2 D. Advanced AI systems, I), p.24-25
paraphrase: Developers of advanced AI should identify, evaluate and mitigate risks across the AI lifecycle.

locator: Part 2 E. Building AI governance, (1), p.26-27
paraphrase: Each actor first conducts an environment and risk analysis of the AI system or service.

locator: Part 3 Code of Conduct, item VI, p.32
